✨The Bioconductor Developers Mentorship Program is back! ✨

Following a successful round in 2022 (iykyk), The Student-ECR Council is
reviving the mentorship program to bring together developers of the
Bioconductor community! Read more about us here
<https://blog.bioconductor.org/posts/2026-08-06-student-ecr-intro/>.

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Do you have a computational tool and you’re not sure how to turn it into a
Bioconductor package?

Do you have previous experience with package development and would like to
pass on your knowledge to the next generation of developers?

This is the program for you! 😄

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Over the course of 6 months, mentees will learn the *fundamentals of
developing a user-friendly and robust package* and/or *submit a candidate
package* to the Bioconductor/Contributions
<https://github.com/Bioconductor/Contributions> GitHub repository with
sufficient advance for review ahead of the following release deadline.
Mentee/mentors will split into small groups and meet over zoom to discuss
various aspects of package development and receive personalised feedback.

*Time commitment for mentors:* Zoom meeting 1h/month. Responding to Zulip
messages outside of meetings is up to the capacity of the individual mentor.

*Time commitment for mentees:* Zoom meeting 1h/month and taking the time
necessary to consistently improve upon the package and actioning feedback.

We are now taking applications for the incoming round: *April 2027 -
October 2027*! 🥳 More information is in the application forms below -

Application form for mentees: https://forms.gle/7kcExTASL8vcTDhr5

Application form for mentors: https://forms.gle/m14YEg1BRbDjBWos5

The deadline to apply is *24 November 2026*. If you have any questions,
please feel free to message in the #student-ecr Zulip channel. Applicants
will be informed of their outcome in February/March 2027.

We hope to see many of you apply! On behalf of the Student-ECR Council,

Carissa

Hi Apratim,

Thank you for your package submission and your patience. As you say, package reviews are done by volunteers and there are a lot of packages in the queue. Your package assignee currently has 6 packages ahead of yours in their queue at this time of writing (github.com/Bioconductor/BiocContributions/issues?q=is%3Aissue+state%3Aopen+assignee%3Ahyu-kim) so a three-week turnaround from submission to review isn't something we can realistically expect. We do our best to get to every submission in the order it was received, but timing depends on reviewer availability.

If you'd like to help speed things up we are always looking for more reviewers. Reviewing is a great way to learn the project's standards and every additional reviewer shortens the wait for everyone, including you, on future submissions. Details on getting involved are here: contributions.bioconductor.org/review-volunteer-chapter.html

Bioconductor is built and maintained by people who give their time freely and the project works best when those who are able also contribute back where they can.

Pariksheet

Hi Kevin,

Sorry for the delay getting back to you.

R Universe uses GitHub actions and GitHub's standard runners,<https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/runners/github-hosted-runners> so we can no longer install system requirements for maintainers.

There are a few ways to deal with system requirements in R Universe for Windows (and macosx).

Where appropriate, it could be bundled with Rtools for Windows and a macosx recipe could be made available at https://github.com/r-macos/recipes. I recommend submitting a recipe for ChemmineOB system requirements. However, Rtools is currently frozen.

Another approach to produce working Windows and macosx binaries is to vendor system requirements, either in the package itself, like Rgraphviz, or in a separate companion package, like Rhtslib/Rsamtools and Rhdf5lib/rhdf5. A separate companion package separates the requirement to a single install that can guarantee compatibility with ChemmineOB for that release. (Thanks to Herv? for this suggestion.) This might be a good approach for ChemmineOB and I recommend looking at those packages.

You might also consider using an agent to facilitate vendoring the system requirements. I also recommend using the R Universe GitHub Action<https://docs.r-universe.dev/bioconductor/#testing-the-build-in-your-own-ci> to test the build. It's easy to set up, runs all the same jobs and on its summary page, the action collects the binaries it produces, which you can download and test.

Given the effort involved and other constraints, you may decide to drop support for an operating system, which you can specify with `Config/Bioconductor/UnsupportedPlatforms<https://contributions.bioconductor.org/advanced-build-options.html?q=unsupp#skipping-builds-on-unsupported-platforms>` in your DESCRIPTION file.

Andres Wokaty (they/them)

Waldron Lab at CUNY SPH

Dear Hong, 

Thank you very much for reporting the buffer overflow vulnerability in LEA and for providing a reproducible example. 

We confirmed the issue and identified a second vulnerable code path in the ANCESTRYMAP conversion routines. Both have now been fixed, and the corrections have passed regression tests and AddressSanitizer checks. 

The fix has been committed and pushed to the Bioconductor development branch (LEA 3.25.1) and is also available on GitHub (bcm-uga/LEA). 

We have also prepared and validated a backport for the current release branch (`RELEASE_3_23`, LEA 3.24.1). However, the push to Bioconductor was rejected with the following message: 

`remote: FATAL: W refs/heads/RELEASE_3_23 packages/LEA olivier.francois DENIED by fallthru` 

To the Bioconductor team (cc): Could you please advise on the appropriate procedure for publishing this security fix to the release branch, or whether additional write permissions are required? 

We are also reviewing related input-validation issues in other conversion routines. 

Thank you again Hong, for bringing this issue to our attention. 

Best regards, 

Olivier François 



De: "Qin, Hong" <hqin at odu.edu> 
À: "Olivier Francois" <olivier.francois at grenoble-inp.fr> 
Envoyé: Mardi 10 Novembre 2026 06:12:15 
Objet: Private report: ancestrymap SNP-name buffer overflow in LEA 



Hello Olivier Francois, 

I am writing to alert you to an ancestrymap name-buffer overflow in LEA identified during our source-verification study. 

We used OpenAI Codex and Anthropic Claude for source analysis, reproduction harnesses, and review of saved test results. Claude designed and ran the static scan; Codex and Claude assisted with verification and source and log audits. 

In version 3.23.0 (Git revision f812da2d3aae5456f0f17776f6ea64fd1de91e88 ), read_line_ancestrymap copies the SNP-name field with strcpy into a 512-byte buffer at src/convert/ancestrymap.c:160. Testing built the package native sources, ran the initializer, and invoked the registered .C entry R_ancestrymap2geno. An unchanged-source adapter reproduced the same copy error. The complete installed-package R workflow has not been tested. 

Source comparisons found the relevant native source unchanged in development version 3.25.0 and inspected release versions 3.22.0 and 3.24.0.

messages.subject_clean: [Bioc-devel] Package review is a lottery: BiocContributions queue numbers
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

How long a new Bioconductor package waits depends less on the code than 
on which reviewer it draws. From the full BiocContributions history 
(until today 12 Nov, 208 assignments):

- Median time to acceptance: 23 to 115 days, depending on the reviewer.
- Median time to first reviewer comment: 9 to 144 days.
- 58 open reviews are older than two months.
- New packages still go to reviewers holding 11 to 14 open reviews, 
while others hold 2 or 3.
- 6 packages have no reviewer at all, one since June.

I believe this is a design problem, not a people problem. Equal intake 
regardless of load means 17 separate queues at very different speeds 
(understandably each reviewer donates different amount of time and effort).

What I propose as a fix:
 ?- One shared queue; push new packages at the end for it; pop the front 
and assign to the next reviewer that has below a cap of open reviews 
(say 4).
 ?- If there is no reviewer comment within say 21 days, then the package 
goes back to the front of the queue.
 ?- Keep hand-picking for packages that need a specialist.
 ?- Publish queue sizes and response times.

We as contributors are expected to follow strict standards and 
deadlines. I believe reviews should meet the same bar. Happy to help 
build this into the workflow.

Best,

--

Hi Lluís, Robert,

I can't speak for whether org.Hs.eg.db will get its PATH map back, but the
NA values come from KEGG's restrictions on redistribution, so I wouldn't
count on it. If what you need is a gene-to-pathway map for examples or
tests, an openly licensed one is easy to get, and I can offer one route.

I've been building bioc-on-ice, which republishes public annotation (NCBI
Gene, GO, Ensembl, HGNC, WikiPathways, and others) as Parquet files plus a
small DuckDB file of views. There's no account and nothing to install
beyond the duckdb R package. Each release sits in a dated folder, so a
vignette can pin one and get the same answer every time. Details and
release notes are here:
https://bioconice.cancerdatasci.org/releases?utm_source=bioc-devel&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=org-hs-eg-db-kegg

KEGG is not in it, for the same licensing reason. WikiPathways is (CC0,
refreshed monthly): 991 human pathways covering 9,031 Entrez genes in the
current release. Reactome (also CC0) is next on the list.

1. A drop-in for as.list(org.Hs.egPATH)
---------------------------------------

library(DBI)
con <- dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb())

  FROM bioc.annotation.wikipathways__gene_pathway gp
  JOIN bioc.annotation.wikipathways__pathway p USING (pathway_id)
  WHERE gp.taxon_id = 9606")

counts pathways per gene. If something really needs an
environment, list2env(egPATH) gives you one.

taxon_id = 9606")

Missatge de Sean Davis <seandavi at gmail.com<mailto:seandavi at gmail.com>> del dia dv., 13 de nov. 2026 a les 18:42:
Hi Lluís, Robert,

I can't speak for whether org.Hs.eg.db will get its PATH map back, but the
NA values come from KEGG's restrictions on redistribution, so I wouldn't
count on it. If what you need is a gene-to-pathway map for examples or
tests, an openly licensed one is easy to get, and I can offer one route.

I've been building bioc-on-ice, which republishes public annotation (NCBI
Gene, GO, Ensembl, HGNC, WikiPathways, and others) as Parquet files plus a
small DuckDB file of views. There's no account and nothing to install
beyond the duckdb R package. Each release sits in a dated folder, so a
vignette can pin one and get the same answer every time. Details and
release notes are here:
https://bioconice.cancerdatasci.org/releases?utm_source=bioc-devel&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=org-hs-eg-db-kegg<https://secure-web.cisco.com/1qQcwY6pHQbHmdPg-kk8Mk6N67lBBgh-_4cT5aRIJreALovYPj_mm-LXI_xJFIZJOtJNFzHyPSgbAZ-wXy_AsMxFccpZ90mT9OOaJPlfMu56qSiDjKg9fu5XEIgQRD9HQemluwtbpmoLV6fBwnuzSCJqZClDMeFVL40DmmX89OOVmW4fgwfzxJO28UGBujDGqRTv3Ti_0hyBQpfLiQ0SsP4qeTgLnBDZfZfCAzGN3h5ZzjTS104bFzUhM_TVagaeicpWyZVpazPdH-AY1kildoFaJI92BDYHliUkXfXEzr7iElYUrRU6qdW1mHDGrUeAT/https%3A%2F%2Fbioconice.cancerdatasci.org%2Freleases%3Futm_source%3Dbioc-devel%26utm_medium%3Demail%26utm_campaign%3Dorg-hs-eg-db-kegg>

KEGG is not in it, for the same licensing reason. WikiPathways is (CC0,
refreshed monthly): 991 human pathways covering 9,031 Entrez genes in the
current release. Reactome (also CC0) is next on the list.

1. A drop-in for as.list(org.Hs.egPATH)
---------------------------------------

library(DBI)
con <- dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb())
dbExecute(con, "INSTALL httpfs; LOAD httpfs;")
dbExecute(con, "ATTACH 'https://data.bioconice.cancerdatasci.org/v2026-11-08/bioconice.duckdb<https://secure-web.cisco.com/1miPRZKQg2F5ys22xMm2YHkV2-kD7uz2_RqRhcs-EZ7mel4wlF7CgsiZ4DBJicRxbzVOg7ZYY09dB4CZ3SOD_VD_hZ7HjOtLFIMOC_kgqNBJfIFClIAn3tm4G6193vOS5PjWdi5FYoHS7cJakIXWLupTmddA4xMOYPcNQb35Oy56Zi3Gu54pYviFqjU-uLBUGZSlcgHV6Z2zJe80FHJou4HpMTz2_0_GuWmlauX_kcCwhl0BiFseOQixHu7CrF1OwncjE1Qs0QBGLbeTI9LJ6zEs5YAggjEbsxrmmn9kP-jcboY-JYJbywcYgGa-0larI/https%3A%2F%2Fdata.bioconice.cancerdatasci.org%2Fv2026-11-08%2Fbioconice.duckdb>'
                AS bioc (READ_ONLY)")

gp <- dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT gp.gene_id, gp.pathway_id, p.name<http://secure-web.cisco.com/1HW6GA4YST_9SQrCu15QlrZK_n47a9JwYMxa028tqJqfD5oIF0zl7xAzl8a2vSI76o0FkTGdJ6-zZuwRds3QNB1N6LO53cKLzSccP8EDu_hKPxJ326_gF03CizxaiIPE5y1KSEvrhW0w0dCfECTKkhdN4OaPWVlivznwkx2wpTOpqWasixlidHD44n16AVqVz2Q1ic6DKSYHfjUSmeYjC95WmIX3bfR3wCoofAqT1gud7QH4HJWVHVP8Bg6CoDKCj2Opxiap5vc7AHwsD4Bkl6gCN6u4YpjiJ9Qwaa342DdS1MFd4kNlnDHQrOIA4uq1e/http%3A%2F%2Fp.name>
  FROM bioc.annotation.wikipathways__gene_pathway gp
  JOIN bioc.annotation.wikipathways__pathway p USING (pathway_id)
  WHERE gp.taxon_id = 9606")
dbDisconnect(con, shutdown = TRUE)

# Same shape as as.list(org.Hs.egPATH): Entrez gene ID -> pathway IDs
egPATH <- split(gp$pathway_id, gp$gene_id)
egPATH[["7157"]]                      # TP53: WP710, WP4754, WP615, ...

# Pathway ID -> name
pathway_names <- unique(gp[, c("pathway_id", "name")])

# Gene sets the way most enrichment tools take them
term2gene <- gp[, c("pathway_id", "gene_id")]       # clusterProfiler::enricher(TERM2GENE = )
pathways  <- split(gp$gene_id, gp$pathway_id)       # fgsea(pathways = )

A named list covers what code usually does with org.Hs.egPATH:
egPATH[keys] replaces mget(keys, org.Hs.egPATH), and lengths(egPATH)
counts pathways per gene. If something really needs an
environment, list2env(egPATH) gives you one.

One caveat: these are different pathways from KEGG's, with different gene
sets. Any enrichment results shown in a vignette will change, not just the
IDs.

The "v2026-11-08" in the URL is the pin. Use "latest" instead to track the
newest release. That host keeps weekly releases for about a month. For
something that has to build for years, like a vignette, use the monthly
archive on Hugging Face instead: each month's release is tagged YYYY-MM
there, and tags are never deleted. The two WikiPathways files are about
360 KB together, so download them rather than querying in place
(anonymous Hugging Face requests are rate-limited):

base <- "https://huggingface.co/datasets/seandavis/bioconice/resolve/2026-11/annotation/"
for (f in c("wikipathways__gene_pathway.parquet", "wikipathways__pathway.parquet"))
  download.file(paste0(base, f), f, mode = "wb")

con <- dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb())
gp <- dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT gp.gene_id, gp.pathway_id, p.name<http://secure-web.cisco.com/1HW6GA4YST_9SQrCu15QlrZK_n47a9JwYMxa028tqJqfD5oIF0zl7xAzl8a2vSI76o0FkTGdJ6-zZuwRds3QNB1N6LO53cKLzSccP8EDu_hKPxJ326_gF03CizxaiIPE5y1KSEvrhW0w0dCfECTKkhdN4OaPWVlivznwkx2wpTOpqWasixlidHD44n16AVqVz2Q1ic6DKSYHfjUSmeYjC95WmIX3bfR3wCoofAqT1gud7QH4HJWVHVP8Bg6CoDKCj2Opxiap5vc7AHwsD4Bkl6gCN6u4YpjiJ9Qwaa342DdS1MFd4kNlnDHQrOIA4uq1e/http%3A%2F%2Fp.name>
  FROM 'wikipathways__gene_pathway.parquet' gp
  JOIN 'wikipathways__pathway.parquet' p USING (pathway_id)
  WHERE gp.taxon_id = 9606")
dbDisconnect(con, shutdown = TRUE)
egPATH <- split(gp$pathway_id, gp$gene_id)

The 2026-11 tag is release 2026-11-01. Its manifest.json lists every
source version that went into it, if you want to cite exactly what you
used. The whole release is browsable at
https://huggingface.co/datasets/seandavis/bioconice?utm_source=bioc-devel&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=org-hs-eg-db-kegg

2. Rolling your own OrgDb with a pathway column
-----------------------------------------------

If you'd rather keep the select()/mapIds() interface, AnnotationForge can
build an org package straight from the same tables. This builds and
installs (I tested it today); the GOALL tables come from your installed
GO.db.

library(DBI)
con <- dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb())
dbExecute(con, "INSTALL httpfs; LOAD httpfs;")
dbExecute(con, "ATTACH 'https://data.bioconice.cancerdatasci.org/v2026-11-08/bioconice.duckdb<https://secure-web.cisco.com/1miPRZKQg2F5ys22xMm2YHkV2-kD7uz2_RqRhcs-EZ7mel4wlF7CgsiZ4DBJicRxbzVOg7ZYY09dB4CZ3SOD_VD_hZ7HjOtLFIMOC_kgqNBJfIFClIAn3tm4G6193vOS5PjWdi5FYoHS7cJakIXWLupTmddA4xMOYPcNQb35Oy56Zi3Gu54pYviFqjU-uLBUGZSlcgHV6Z2zJe80FHJou4HpMTz2_0_GuWmlauX_kcCwhl0BiFseOQixHu7CrF1OwncjE1Qs0QBGLbeTI9LJ6zEs5YAggjEbsxrmmn9kP-jcboY-JYJbywcYgGa-0larI/https%3A%2F%2Fdata.bioconice.cancerdatasci.org%2Fv2026-11-08%2Fbioconice.duckdb>'
                AS bioc (READ_ONLY)")
q <- function(sql) dbGetQuery(con, sql)

# makeOrgPackage rules: each table's first column is GID, and the other
# column names become select() columns, so they must be unique.
gene_info <- q("SELECT DISTINCT gene_id AS GID, symbol AS SYMBOL, description AS GENENAME
                FROM bioc.annotation.ncbi__gene WHERE taxon_id = 9606")
chromosome <- q("SELECT DISTINCT gene_id AS GID, chromosome AS CHR
                 FROM bioc.annotation.ncbi__gene
                 WHERE taxon_id = 9606 AND chromosome IS NOT NULL")
go <- q("SELECT DISTINCT gene_id AS GID, go_id AS GO, evidence AS EVIDENCE
         FROM bioc.annotation.ncbi__gene_go WHERE taxon_id = 9606")
wikipathways <- q("SELECT DISTINCT gene_id AS GID, pathway_id AS WIKIPATHWAYS
                   FROM bioc.annotation.wikipathways__gene_pathway WHERE taxon_id = 9606")
xref <- function(ns) q(sprintf(
  "SELECT DISTINCT source_id AS GID, target_id AS %s
   FROM bioc.annotation.identifier_mapping
   WHERE taxon_id = 9606 AND source_namespace = 'ENTREZ' AND target_namespace = '%s'",
  ns, ns))
alias <- xref("ALIAS"); ensembl <- xref("ENSEMBL")
uniprot <- xref("UNIPROT"); omim <- xref("OMIM")
dbDisconnect(con, shutdown = TRUE)   # run every query before this line

AnnotationForge::makeOrgPackage(
  gene_info = gene_info, chromosome = chromosome, go = go,
  alias = alias, ensembl = ensembl, uniprot = uniprot, omim = omim,
  wikipathways = wikipathways,
  version = "0.0.1", maintainer = "You <you at example.org<mailto:you at example.org>>", author = "You",
  outputDir = ".", tax_id = "9606", genus = "Homo", species = "sapiens",
  goTable = "go")

install.packages("org.Hsapiens.eg.db", repos = NULL, type = "source")
library(org.Hsapiens.eg.db)
select(org.Hsapiens.eg.db, keys = "TP53", keytype = "SYMBOL",
       columns = c("GID", "WIKIPATHWAYS"))

# The org.Hs.egPATH-style list, from the OrgDb
egPATH <- mapIds(org.Hsapiens.eg.db, keys(org.Hsapiens.eg.db, "GID"),
                 column = "WIKIPATHWAYS", keytype = "GID", multiVals = "list")
egPATH <- egPATH[!vapply(egPATH, function(v) all(is.na<http://secure-web.cisco.com/1xB8TVK1g4cEV6DZYmhdz3K_4REVYDkREsszp3pdJxGMicW1vt4YmjjqmqaNCdzq93JSHBqtLXi3mBxScmbXT3nr4YnFbyWQnNE3Ex7OCp8PYAUw2f4DS5Gl1hQKtQ1Ohf-PnwQ5gPRD9M6kLZrrtqnvCuzQsUFW3v8vY9gUF6GqMYN1s2uZTDpRkU0713-Qignyyfei_3oFHpt3nYCS29jAVyGeN-PNm6Zq6Rx9pLrVZQ1A68zcmvrwiJZRk536VomBHIMSf_khWG8W2vimaK9xY_Id3D9jAvKAcs0q7TnM_hXq3fNM4Sv-M_YZ3AXE-/http%3A%2F%2Fis.na>(v)), TRUE)]

Things that tripped me up:

- The key column is GID, not ENTREZID. That's how makeOrgPackage names it,
  so code that hardcodes keytype = "ENTREZID" needs a change.
- Packages built this way have the OrgDb object only, no org.Xx.egPATH
  style bimaps. Those come only with the official org packages. mapIds()
  as above gives you the same list.
- The installed package is about 750 MB, almost all of it the GOALL
  tables. Drop go/goTable if you only need pathways.
- GOALL is computed from your local GO.db. If that GO release differs from
  the one NCBI's gene2go used, some terms can drop out of the ancestor
  closure.

If you need KEGG itself and you're fine with KEGG's terms, KEGGREST will
fetch it at run time. For a vignette that has to build on the build
machines, I'd avoid the network dependency.

Happy to help if either of you tries this and hits a snag.

Sean

messages.subject: [Bioc-devel] Retrospective bio
messages.body_plain:
Dear Lori,

With the greatest of respect, I don't it is wise or reasonable to introduce a retrospective requirement with just 3 days notice that all historical Bioconductor packages suddenly have to pass BiocCheck on R-Universe. As far as I know, this requirement has not been discussed before for existing packages.

Bioconductor packages have always been required to pass R CMD check, which does indeed check code correctness, and that is good and fine. I have always found that helpful. BiocCheck however consists mainly of stylistic requirements that are subjective and which programmers other than the BiocCheck authors might not agree with. I personally find some of the requirements to be arbitrary and simplistic.

A great many of the most highly cited Bioconductor packages are now stamped with an "ERROR" in red capital letters on their R-universe landing page. That includes limma, edgeR, DESeq2 and many, many others, including packages such as IRanges that are maintained by the Biocore team and even Biobase itself.

IMO, it is a very bad look. It gives the impression that the community now has no confidence in the most highly cited and important Bioconductor packages
that have made Bioconductor famous around the world over the past 25 years. How would a potential Bioconductor user interpret that, or indeed an assessor evaluating a Bioconductor grant application?

The limma package comes with a 151 page User's Guide and a 264 page reference manual built from 177 help files that include 87 runnable examples. Some might consider that good but, no, it is ERROR from BiocCheck because there are not enough runnable examples. limma might have more runnable examples than any other Bioconductor package but still not enough!  Meanwhile, a toy package with a half page reference manual and one runnable example, no matter how trivial, would be considered perfect. limma includes many Rd files for which a runnable example would be inappropriate, impossible or wasteful. Ironically, I could make limma pass BioCheck by deleting half the help files, but I am not willing to do that.

BTW, I am a bit confused by the fact that each Bioconductor package now has two landing pages, one on bioconductor.org and one on R-universe. What is the role of the two pages going forward? R-universe has a strong github social programming orientation, which is not a direction that I necessarily want to go in, especially in this new AI era.

I see you have advised Yang Liao that the R-Universe BiocCheck requirement will not be strictly enforced this Friday, but will still be enforced "gradually". That makes it sound as if we are tolerated "for now", but may get reevaluated at any time. Personally, I want to maintain my software in a way that seems to me to be best for users and best for my team, rather than fitting in with arbitrary rules that don't improve the code performance.

Best wishes
Gordon

Professor Gordon K Smyth
Lab Head, Technology Sciences Division, WEHI

messages.body_plain:
I agree with Gordon's sentiments.

Several packages I maintain have BiocCheck ERRORs because some help 
pages don't have runnable examples. But why do they all need runnable 
examples? Some help pages document abstract concepts that are referenced 
by other pages, e.g., descriptions of virtual classes; or deprecated, 
defunct, or re-exported functions, for which examples are inappropriate; 
or low-level utilities that end-users shouldn't be calling but are 
exported for use in other packages of the same suite, e.g., alabaster. 
It seems silly to raise an ERROR because we don't meet some arbitrary 
threshold for runnable examples.

Off the top of my head, the only (somewhat) useful "ERROR" that 
BiocCheck emits is whether the maintainer is watching the relevant tags 
on the support site. Many of my packages don't pass this check - at some 
point, the support site limited the number of watchable tags, so I had 
to delete some in order to make space for new tags. But in any case, 
this is a poor mechanism to enforce compliance. You already have the 
maintainer email for each package, you already know how to match it to 
the maintainer's support site account, and you have admin access to the 
support site. Why not just have a scheduled job that automatically adds 
all appropriate tags to the maintainer's support site account? Then 
there's no need for this check at all, which is one less thing for 
maintainers to worry about.

As for coding style: I just ignore most of BiocCheck's NOTEs. I don't 
need to be told how to format my own code, and frankly, I don't see why 
it's Bioconductor's business. I'm not asking the core team to maintain 
my packages, so if I'm the only one who interacts with the source, I 
should be able to write it as I wish. (Occasional commits by Herve to 
update function calls don't count as "maintenance", at least not to the 
extent that I have to restyle my code to be more "readable" to whoever 
set these rules.)

I appreciate BiocCheck's role in guiding new developers who don't know

messages.body_plain:
I'm sorry I didn't explain this in my email out to people for this release but we are NOT requiring BiocCheck at this point.

As I mentioned in this post:
https://stat.ethz.ch/pipermail/bioc-devel/2026-November/021608.html


Until R-universe, we only ran BiocCheck on incoming packages,
now that we have the ability to run these checks on all packages we have begun doing so and are reporting the results.
We will evaluate the checks and slowly implement enforcement or modify or remove accordingly now that we have
Data on it. We could not refine something that we could not run in bulk.

Many were introduced as you said to help new developers (things like coding style) where at the time and still do occasionally receive packages that had no consistent syntax and made it impossible to review.  Suggesting good practices as a NOTE that can be ignored.  Perhaps this could be revisited but many others have found it helpful.

We can evaluate the right threshold for examples. Bioconductor has always insisted on runnable code in the vignette, runnable examples, and tests.  I too personally feel this check should be better and take into account all of these. But that is also what makes Bioconductor standards; ensuring the package functions actually run (at least somewhere, at least once). Again now that we have better data we can refine and better it.

We will be removing the support site shortly as we will be transitioning to a new system.  (Not yet announced and we will provide details when appropriate to the community about this switch). And as you can also understand signing people up for mailing lists they didn't do themselves could also cause major controversy and seem intrusive.

As far as two landing pages that is unavoidable but needed.
R-universe has its own mechanisms for distributing packages and we will be making a larger blog post, and mailing list and social media post around R-universe in the near future.
But Bioconductor still requires additional checks for propagation that R-universe does not.  The Bioconductor landing pages are the versions and packages that are endorsed and officially distributed by Bioconductor.  The R-Universe landing page is for evaluating the build results.  We eventually will be releasing tools and ability to view package build results in different ways (and in bulk for maintainers of multiple packages), in addition to the R-universe page.

It is not our intention to alienate or discourage our long term contributors and hopefully this helps easy the concern. There will be large announcements and details forth coming about the transitions that should clarify.



Lori Kern

Bioconductor Core Team

Roswell Park Comprehensive Cancer Center

Department of Biostatistics & Bioinformatics

Elm & Carlton Streets

Buffalo, New York 14263

Sent: Wednesday, November 18, 2026 12:31 AM
To: bioc-devel at r-project.org <bioc-devel at r-project.org>
Subject: Re: [Bioc-devel] Retrospective bio

I agree with Gordon's sentiments.

Several packages I maintain have BiocCheck ERRORs because some help
pages don't have runnable examples. But why do they all need runnable
examples? Some help pages document abstract concepts that are referenced
by other pages, e.g., descriptions of virtual classes; or deprecated,
defunct, or re-exported functions, for which examples are inappropriate;
or low-level utilities that end-users shouldn't be calling but are
exported for use in other packages of the same suite, e.g., alabaster.
It seems silly to raise an ERROR because we don't meet some arbitrary
threshold for runnable examples.

Off the top of my head, the only (somewhat) useful "ERROR" that
BiocCheck emits is whether the maintainer is watching the relevant tags
on the support site. Many of my packages don't pass this check - at some
point, the support site limited the number of watchable tags, so I had
to delete some in order to make space for new tags. But in any case,
this is a poor mechanism to enforce compliance. You already have the
maintainer email for each package, you already know how to match it to
the maintainer's support site account, and you have admin access to the
support site. Why not just have a scheduled job that automatically adds
all appropriate tags to the maintainer's support site account? Then
there's no need for this check at all, which is one less thing for
maintainers to worry about.

As for coding style: I just ignore most of BiocCheck's NOTEs. I don't
need to be told how to format my own code, and frankly, I don't see why
it's Bioconductor's business. I'm not asking the core team to maintain
my packages, so if I'm the only one who interacts with the source, I
should be able to write it as I wish. (Occasional commits by Herve to
update function calls don't count as "maintenance", at least not to the
extent that I have to restyle my code to be more "readable" to whoever
set these rules.)

I appreciate BiocCheck's role in guiding new developers who don't know
any better. But that's all it should do.

-A

Bioconductor has always had the ability to run checks on all packages at regular intervals:
<https://bioconductor.org/checkResults/devel/bioc-LATEST/>
and BiocCheck style checks could have been included at any time had they been considered appropriate (which until now they weren't).

You don't say in your email, but am I right to guess that there is a plan to abandon Bioconductor's checkResults and instead depend entirely on R-universe?

R CMD checks on on R-universe are actually lighter than those on Bioconductor (--no-manual, --no-vignettes) and cannot be viewed on the site. They can only be downloaded as a zip, separately for each platform. I don't think they will be ever be viewed by authors who submit low quality packages to Bioconductor with no consistent syntax.

Bioc checking has always been focused on small packages that do easy things over large packages that do difficult things on large datasets, which to me is what Bioconductor should aspire to be about. Yesterday, an international visitor came up to me at a conference to say how important the limma User's Guide has been to him over the years. Yet the User's Guide is fundamentally incompatible with Bioconductor's rules for runnable code in vignettes.

Gordon

> site. They can only be downloaded as a zip, separately for each platform. I
> don't think they will be ever be viewed by authors who submit low quality
> packages to Bioconductor with no consistent syntax.
>
> Bioc checking has always been focused on small packages that do easy
> things over large packages that do difficult things on large datasets,
> which to me is what Bioconductor should aspire to be about. Yesterday, an
> international visitor came up to me at a conference to say how important
> the limma User's Guide has been to him over the years. Yet the User's Guide
> is fundamentally incompatible with Bioconductor's rules for runnable code
> in vignettes.
>

Thanks Gordon.  I have a few points in response to various elements in the
thread; specifically I would dispute
"actually lighter" above, and other points, but perhaps this list will be
useful:

1.  There is no retrospective requirement of status with BiocCheck.

2.  BiocCheck is open source software that raises developer awareness of
opportunities for quality improvement.  Opinions may differ on what
constitutes an improvement.  Community proposals for enhancement are
welcome.

3.  BiocCheck events are not proposed as indicators of project health to
be evaluated by funders.  See impact.bioconductor.org for indicators of
project
health and scope that funders would be wise to evaluate.  This resource
was built by Sean Davis.  Please be acquainted with it and direct your
funders to it.

4.  Multiple points of entry to bioconductor package metadata have long
been available: landing pages, build report entries, GitHub repository
issue streams, pkgdown sites, support site, r-universe pages.  One or
two more are unlikely to impair user or developer experience but we
welcome further discussion of the point.

5.  Our use of R-universe for scalable build-check-distribute processes
was enabled by extensive collaborative development by Jeroen Ooms and bioc
core members.  Infrastructure sources are all in the open, as they have
always
been.  Extensive effort by core members has been undertaken to minimize
disruptions involved with this essential transition.  Particular effort
has been devoted to maintaining the level of package checking prior to
distribution historically employed by the Bioconductor project.

6.  Among factual points that might be revised, I would point out that
the claim that the limma "User's Guide is fundamentally incompatible
with Bioconductor's rules for runnable code in vignettes" is not correct.
The guide is indeed breathtaking in scope but of the same order of
complexity and data-richness as several books that are now in the
build system.  With suitable mock and cached data elements the
content could be formed into a fully compliant and checkable
vignette.  If you are interested in this, please let us know.

7.  It has been observed that the tone of some remarks in this thread
verges towards dismissiveness and disrespect for project personnel,
collaborators, and their work.

8.  Gordon and Aaron, we admire you and your intellectual and
technical progeny and would never deliberately do anything to make
your work more difficult.  Let's hope the continuation of this discussion
leads
to improved experiences for all Bioconductor users and contributors.

messages.body_plain:
Please remember to update your NEWS files for any information about changes to your packages during this last development cycle.  Bioconductor collates all package news files as part of the release announcement. If your NEWS file is not formatted correctly and not updated by this weekend, it will not be included in the release announcement.

For clarification:
The release 3.24 branch has not yet been created.  Please continue to update the devel branch.
Next week when the release occurs the core team will automatically create the RELEASE_3_24 branch on git.bioconductor.org but until that time the only branch accessible is devel.  Do NOT try to create a RELEASE_3_24 branch on your own; the core team will do this for you.  Bioconductor will also handle bumping the y of a package version x.y.z accordingly.

There will be a freeze of the devel branch at noon ET on Monday November 23. The devel branch will be frozen for several hours while the core team creates the RELEASE_3_24 and bump versions accordingly.  We will announce this freeze and when the freeze is lifted on the mailing list.


Cheers,
